report:
## Research Summary

The claim traces largely to a single, widely-cited trial: Manber et al. (2010), a randomized controlled trial in *Obstetrics & Gynecology* comparing depression-specific acupuncture, a non-specific ("control") acupuncture, and massage in 150 pregnant women with major depressive disorder. Depression-specific acupuncture produced significantly greater symptom reduction and higher response rates than the control conditions, and the authors concluded it "could be a viable treatment option" (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/2010/03000/acupuncture_for_depression_during_pregnancy__a.7.aspx; https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2010/02/acupuncture-lessens-depression-symptoms-during-pregnancy-study-shows.html). Notably, the lead author herself noted this result runs counter to studies in non-pregnant populations, where depression-specific acupuncture has not outperformed placebo/sham acupuncture, and she could not fully explain the discrepancy (https://health.usnews.com/health-news/blogs/on-women/2010/02/22/acupuncture-may-help-alleviate-depression-during-pregnancy).

Subsequent evidence is thinner and mixed. A 2016 Australian pragmatic RCT protocol described only "preliminary evidence" as "suggestive" that acupuncture may help, explicitly calling for more research before conclusions could be drawn (https://researchers.mq.edu.au/en/publications/evaluation-of-an-antenatal-acupuncture-intervention-as-an-adjunct/). Reviews of acupuncture for postpartum (rather than antenatal) depression similarly find effects "inconclusive," citing small samples, heterogeneous methods, and risk of bias (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9371482/).

**Conclusion:** The claim is not simply false, but it is overstated. One credible RCT found benefit specifically during pregnancy, but it is a single moderate-sized study whose result is inconsistent with broader acupuncture-depression research and hasn't been robustly replicated. The evidence is preliminary/mixed rather than definitively confirming or debunking the claim—"unproven" is more accurate than "false."
